summary: Initial POC scoping focused on how Redwood will handle prompt telemetry, PII redaction, retention settings, and benchmarking for Synergy AI's customer support assistant. Customer needs: no raw prompt storage for PII, short retention for telemetry, ability to run on Dedicated or Private depending on SLA, and measurable latency/cost targets. Agreed next steps to exchange sample traffic, run a 10k token benchmark, and iterate on retention configs and redaction rules.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 16:05 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Synergy AI), Daniel Park (Platform Eng), Sasha Reed (CISO), Alex Gomez (NLP Lead)

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:12] Priya (Synergy AI): Priya here.
[00:14] Daniel: Daniel.
[00:15] Sasha: Sasha on.
[00:16] Alex: Alex.
[00:18] Liam (Redwood SE): Liam here.
[00:20] Maya: Cool. I've put the agenda in the invite: POC scope around prompt telemetry, retention, redaction, benchmarks, and timelines. We'll try to leave 10 minutes at the end for questions.

[00:35] Priya: Great, to give quick context: we're building a support assistant that will see user messages and some backend context. Our legal team is pretty strict on PII — ideally we don't want raw prompts persisted. We also need a small footprint for telemetry, like only sampling 5% of conversations for QA but retaining aggregated metrics for 90 days.

[01:05] Maya: Understood. Liam, want to walk through how Redwood can handle no-store and redaction options?

[01:12] Liam: Yeah — so high level we support a few patterns. One is no-store at the platform layer: requests can be marked no_persist which avoids writing prompts to long-term stores, we only keep ephemeral KV cache for inference. Second is token-level or field-level redaction pre-ingest — you can call the SDK with a redaction mask or we can run an inline PII detector to replace values with placeholders. Third is encrypted prompt storage: if you need to keep them for debugging, we can store encrypted artifacts behind customer KMS and limited TTL.

[01:45] Sasha: Two questions — how reliable is the inline PII detector? And what about audit logs for compliance?

[01:53] Liam: The detector is model-based — it catches common patterns (emails, SSNs, credit cards) with about 92% precision in our internal tests, but there are edge cases. For compliance, we provide audit logs that show request IDs, which model variant served, and whether redaction/no-store flags were applied. We don't include decrypted content in the audit logs unless you explicitly enable debug retention.

[02:30] Daniel: Can that 92% be tuned? We have domain-specific entities (account IDs with weird formats).

[02:36] Liam: Yes. We can run a short tuning pass during the POC: you provide annotated examples and we can add rule-based heuristics to the detector for those account patterns. That would be part of a two-week POC tuning milestone.

[03:05] Alex: How does this affect latency? Our SLA target is P95 < 400ms end-to-end for short prompts (<= 64 tokens).

[03:13] Liam: Inline detector adds a small sync step — usually 30–60ms per request for our optimized detector. If you need sub-200ms latency we recommend a pre-filter that runs client-side or a lightweight regex-based preprocessor to remove common tokens, with the heavier model-based detector used only for sampled traffic. Also Dedicated or Private deployments give lower tail latencies because you avoid noisy neighbors.

[03:50] Priya: Let's talk retention: we want telemetry (latency, token counts, error rates) retained for 90 days in full, but we want raw prompt content kept no longer than 24 hours unless encrypted and authorized. Is that doable?

[04:05] Maya: Yes — we have configurable retention policies. For hosted API you can set retention TTL and sampling rates. For Private, you control the storage plugins and encryption with your KMS. We'll show a sample retention config in the follow-up.

[04:25] Sasha: Who has access to the decrypted prompts if we enable short-term retention for debugging?

[04:30] Liam: Access is role-based: only users with the debug role and explicit audit justification can retrieve. All retrievals are logged and we support single-use keys for debug sessions. We can integrate with your SSO for RBAC.

[05:00] Priya: About telemetry sampling — you mentioned sampling 5%. We want the sampling to be stratified by customer tier and error state, not purely random. Can Redwood do that?

[05:10] Liam: Yes, sampling policies can be defined on request attributes — you can always up-sample for failed responses or VIP customers. We'll ship policy templates in the POC repo.

[05:35] Maya: Moving to workload sizing — Priya, what peak QPS and token-per-request numbers should we plan for?

[05:42] Priya: We're seeing spikes up to 45 QPS during peak hours, median around 12 QPS. Average prompt is 40 tokens, responses about 80 tokens. We expect about 3 million tokens/day.

[06:00] Liam: Ok that maps to a small Dedicated pool — likely 4xA1-like GPUs (approx), but we'll do exact benchmarking. For POC we can simulate your traffic shape and run cost/latency curves on our hosted infra and a dedicated preview cluster.

[06:25] Daniel: For the POC bench, what do you need from our side?

[06:28] Maya: Sample traffic and PII schema please — anonymized. Also define success criteria: latency targets, throughput, and an acceptable cost per 1k tokens.

[06:37] Priya: Success criteria: P95 latency < 400ms, 99th < 750ms on Dedicated mode; no raw prompt retention beyond 24 hours in hosted; telemetry retained 90 days; PII redaction recall above 95% on the tuned detector; and cost target less than $0.25 per 1k tokens (we'll accept a range during POC).

[07:05] Alex: About benchmarks — can you produce token-level breakdowns so we can compare against our internal baseline?

[07:10] Liam: Yes we'll provide token-level latency histograms, per-route cost, and a KV cache hit-rate analysis. We'll also include a prefix-caching scenario since your assistant repeats a large system prompt.

[07:45] Maya: There was a question earlier about where prompts are stored when using streaming responses — Liam?

[07:50] Liam: For streaming we keep an ephemeral buffer in memory during the session; nothing is flushed to blob storage unless you enable logs or debug retention. If you use function-calling or structured output we'll store the parsed function args per your retention policy.

[08:20] Sasha: Encryption — can you integrate with our cloud KMS (GCP KMS) so that stored prompts are encrypted under our key?

[08:30] Liam: Yes, Private and Dedicated support customer-managed KMS integrations. For hosted we support envelope encryption where root keys are customer-managed. We'll include the KMS integration guide in the security pack.

[09:00] Priya: A small operational ask: during POC can we get a monthly ingestion cap alert? We want to avoid accidental cost spikes.

[09:07] Maya: Yep, usage alerts and soft caps are part of the console — we'll pre-configure a cap for the POC and share access to the cost dashboard.

[09:25] Daniel: About redaction logs — we need to be able to prove to auditors that PII was redacted. Can logs show redaction decisions without exposing content?

[09:33] Liam: Logs include redaction metadata: rule id, redaction mask, and request id. The actual redacted content in logs will be masked by default. If auditors need decrypted evidence, that's a separate controlled flow with audit trails.

[10:00] [10:00–28:00] — technical deep-dive (Liam leads):
[10:00] Liam: I'll outline our PII pipeline: pre-ingest detection -> redaction masks -> tokenization-aware masking to avoid leaking partial tokens -> optional deterministic pseudonymization for keys that need correlation across requests.
[10:30] Alex: Deterministic pseudonymization: how do you handle collisions?
[10:35] Liam: We namespace with customer-specific salts stored in KMS and a truncation-safe hash. Collisions are possible but extremely unlikely; we can add suffix indexing if you need absolute uniqueness.

[11:10] Priya: For debugging, we sometimes need to replay a conversation end-to-end. How do you support replays without violating retention?

[11:18] Liam: We support single-use debug snapshots: you can request a replay token, which triggers a policy check and creates an encrypted snapshot with a 24-hour single-use TTL. All accesses are logged to an immutable audit log.

[12:00] Maya: Quick note — for the POC we'll run two benchmark passes: one on hosted with privacy flags enabled, one on a small dedicated preview cluster. The hosted run will validate retention/no-store; the dedicated run will evaluate tail latency and cost.

[12:25] Daniel: For the hosted run, will the no-store flag truly prevent data from being used to improve models? We need to ensure no downstream training uses the prompts.

[12:32] Liam: No-store ensures data is not written to training pipelines. We also provide contractual assurances in the data processing addendum. We'll put the DPA excerpt in the security pack.

[13:00] Priya: Timeline — we have a vendor selection window by end of Q2. We'd like a POC done in 3 weeks, but realistic?

[13:08] Maya: Realistically, with your samples and quick sign-off on security docs, we can run a 3-week POC: week 1 ingest + detector tuning, week 2 hosted benchmark + retention test, week 3 dedicated benchmark + wrap-up. If rule-tuning goes long it might expand to 4 weeks.

[13:40] Sasha: We need to loop in legal for the DPA and a short security questionnaire. Can you share an SOC2 summary and encryption flow?

[13:48] Maya: Yes — security pack will contain SOC 2 attestation, encryption diagrams, KMS integration steps, RBAC screenshots, and an example retention policy.

[14:10] Alex: On the benchmarking specifics — can you show us per-model variant perf? We run a custom small model and a medium one; we want to know how quantization modes affect P95 latency.

[14:20] Liam: We'll include run matrices for full precision vs int8 quantized variants and show latency/cost tradeoffs. We'll also include model warm-up effects and KV cache hit rates.

[15:00] Maya: Any other concerns?

[15:06] Daniel: One minor thing — our network blocks outbound traffic to some telemetry endpoints; how do we handle pushing metrics back to our observability stack?

[15:14] Liam: You can either push via a secure private endpoint over the VPC peering or we can ship metrics via an agent that writes into your telemetry collector. We'll work with your infra to pick the approach.

[15:40] Priya: Recap then: we want POC scope doc, sample traffic, security pack, bench runs on hosted and dedicated, detector tuning, and a follow-up infra deep-dive.

[15:55] Maya: Yep. I'll send the POC playbook + security pack by Friday (2026-03-06). Liam will share a benchmark script and expected dataset format. Priya to provide traffic and PII patterns by Monday (2026-03-08). We'll aim to start run 1 the week of 2026-03-09.

[16:15] Sasha: Sounds good. One last ask — can the POC include a small compliance dashboard widget showing retention state per artifact?

[16:22] Liam: We can prototype a retention UI that shows counts by TTL bucket and redaction rate. We'll include screenshots in the deliverable.

[16:35] Maya: Thanks all. We'll follow up in email with attachments.
[16:40] Priya: Thanks.
[16:42] Alex: Thanks everyone.
[16:45] Meeting end.

Notes on transcription: some speaker labels merged (e.g., "Maya" vs "Speaker 1" in raw), occasional mishears ("kvcash" instead of KV cache, "vice pea see"), filled pauses and overlap removed in a couple places for readability.
